prompt: A payment worker container disappears during a traffic spike. The host still reports 18 GiB available memory. `docker container inspect` shows `ExitCode=137`, `OOMKilled=true`, a 512 MiB memory limit, no restart policy, and a writable container layer that grew by 3 GiB. The last application log says only `batch started`; there is no graceful-shutdown message. An operator says, 'The host was not out of memory, so Docker must have randomly killed it. Increase the limit to 4 GiB and restart.' Diagnose the event from first principles. Explain exit status, signal and cgroup evidence, filesystem growth, containment, recovery, verification, and prevention without assuming that one symptom proves the full root cause.
directAnswer: The strongest current mechanism evidence is a cgroup-scoped out-of-memory kill, not host-wide exhaustion: `OOMKilled=true` is runtime evidence for this container, status 137 commonly represents 128 plus SIGKILL 9, and a 512 MiB cgroup can exhaust while the host still has free memory. SIGKILL cannot run application cleanup, which explains the missing graceful log but does not reveal why memory grew. The 3 GiB writable layer is a separate storage signal and may be logs/cache/temp data; it did not directly consume the 512 MiB memory limit, although I/O or page-cache behavior can interact. Freeze blind restarts, preserve inspect/cgroup/application/runtime evidence, quantify unfinished and duplicate work, reproduce with the same image/config, and identify memory.current/peak/events plus workload allocation and queue behavior. Recover only idempotent or reconciled batches with bounded concurrency. Change the limit only after measuring a justified working set and node headroom, while fixing the leak/unbounded batch or backpressure defect, adding graceful checkpointing, restart policy/controller ownership, read-only rootfs plus bounded writable mounts, and alerts on working set, OOM events, layer growth, queue age, and verified batch outcomes.
foundation: A container is a set of host processes constrained and viewed through namespaces and cgroups; it is not a small virtual machine with its own kernel. A memory cgroup can enforce a 512 MiB limit even when the host has many free GiB. If the kernel kills a process with SIGKILL, a shell often reports 137 because 128 + signal number 9 = 137. That arithmetic is a clue, while the runtime's OOMKilled flag and cgroup memory events are stronger scoped evidence. SIGKILL cannot be caught, so `finally`, traps, and graceful logs do not run. A container writable layer stores changed image paths and is normally ephemeral; growing it can exhaust Docker storage or slow copy-on-write independently of the memory limit. Restarting may repeat incomplete work unless operations are idempotent or reconciled.
reasoningSteps: State user impact first: which batches, payments, tenants, and time window are incomplete, duplicated, or unknown. Preserve the logical job and item identities before any restart.

Record exact container ID, image reference and image ID/digest, created/start/finish times, runtime state, exit code, OOMKilled flag, restart count, health, configured command, user, mounts, limits, and code/config revision.
Interpret exit 137 as conventionally 128 plus signal 9, then corroborate. Exit codes can be produced explicitly or wrapped by supervisors; do not diagnose OOM from 137 alone.

Use `OOMKilled=true`, cgroup `memory.events`/`memory.events.local`, memory limit, peak/current metrics, and kernel/runtime events to establish whether this cgroup experienced an OOM kill. State which cgroup and time window produced each observation.

Explain why 18 GiB host-available memory does not disprove cgroup exhaustion. The container's hierarchical limit, node reservations, parent cgroups, swap policy, and reclaim behavior are distinct capacity boundaries.

Separate trigger from root cause. Traffic may trigger growth; root cause can be unbounded batch materialization, retained objects, queue concurrency, child processes, cache, memory leak, request size, or a limit below the legitimate measured working set.

Treat missing graceful shutdown as expected under SIGKILL, not evidence the application ignored SIGTERM. Review whether PID 1 forwards TERM, whether stop grace is sufficient, and whether durable work state survives abrupt death.

Investigate the 3 GiB writable layer independently using container diff/size and exact paths before removal. Determine whether files are logs, cache, downloads, temp data, or state; check Docker backing-store capacity and inode use.

Contain by stopping uncontrolled restart loops, reducing admission/concurrency, protecting healthy tenants, preserving the failed container and logs if policy permits, and establishing a bounded replacement cohort with the exact known image digest.

Reconcile every in-flight item at its authoritative owner. Mark committed, absent, rejected, duplicate, or unknown; retry only idempotent or proven-absent eligible work with stable identity and a time/attempt budget.

Recover with an evidence-based memory request/limit and node headroom, not an arbitrary 4 GiB. Add backpressure and smaller batches first where possible. Abort if OOM events, queue age, duplicates, or node pressure rise.

Verify the original user operations, not merely container running state: all items terminal, no duplicates, queue drains, memory reaches a stable envelope under representative load, no new OOM events, writable growth bounded, and shutdown/restart behavior tested.

Prevent with memory profiling, realistic load/failure tests, cgroup-aware telemetry, bounded concurrency/input/buffers, checkpoint/idempotency design, read-only rootfs, explicit tmpfs/volume size policy, stdout/stderr logging, non-root execution, resource declarations, health semantics, and controller-aware rollout.
seniorAnswer: I would declare the worker outcome and any in-flight payment batch unknown, stop automatic replay, and preserve the exact container/runtime/cgroup evidence. Host free memory is not the governing limit: this container was configured for 512 MiB. Exit 137 suggests SIGKILL, while `OOMKilled=true` plus a matching cgroup `oom_kill` increment and timestamps would establish a cgroup OOM mechanism for this instance. That still does not identify the allocation defect. I would correlate memory current/peak, working set, anonymous/file/slab categories where available, process RSS, child count, batch size, concurrency, queue depth, request distribution, and code revision. SIGKILL explains why no graceful handler ran. Separately, I would inventory the 3 GiB writable layer by exact path and Docker backing-store usage; persistent business state in that layer is a design bug, but layer growth is not automatically the memory OOM cause. Containment caps intake and retries, preserves operation IDs, and runs a small known-digest canary. Recovery reconciles every item at the payment owner before retry and uses a measured request/limit with node safety margin. I would fix unbounded allocation or concurrency, make work resumable/idempotent, ensure PID 1 receives TERM for planned stops, use a read-only root with bounded explicit mounts, stream logs, and alert on verified job failure, OOM events, memory saturation/peak, restart amplification, queue age, and container-layer growth. Success is correct payment outcomes under representative load and interruption, not a container that stays up after assigning 4 GiB.
weakAnswer: Exit 137 always means Docker ran out of host RAM. Give the container 4 GiB, enable restart always, and delete its large files.
whyWeak: Exit 137 alone is not unique proof, the relevant limit is cgroup-scoped, an arbitrary increase can move pressure to the node, restart can duplicate unknown work, and deleting files destroys evidence or state without proving ownership. It conflates memory and writable-layer storage and ignores PID 1, reconciliation, capacity measurement, user verification, and prevention.

evidence.signal: The exact container instance has `OOMKilled=true`; its cgroup memory limit is 536,870,912 bytes and `memory.events` shows an `oom_kill` increment in the incident window.
evidence.proves: The kernel/runtime recorded a memory-cgroup OOM kill for that scoped workload under the observed limit.
evidence.doesNotProve: Which allocation path caused growth, whether the limit was wrong, or the correctness of payment outcomes.

evidence.signal: The host had 18 GiB available while the container cgroup approached its 512 MiB maximum.
evidence.proves: Host aggregate availability and this container's enforced capacity were different boundaries.
evidence.doesNotProve: That the host had no other pressure, parent cgroup constraint, reclaim stall, or reservation issue.

evidence.signal: The runtime records signal-derived exit 137 and no graceful application log, while a controlled TERM test logs cleanup and exits zero.
evidence.proves: Abrupt and graceful paths differ in the tested build and supports SIGKILL bypassing cleanup in this event.
evidence.doesNotProve: That every shutdown path works, or why the OOM occurred.

evidence.signal: Container filesystem inventory attributes 3 GiB of writable-layer growth to an application cache, while memory profiling attributes peak anonymous memory to an unbounded batch list.
evidence.proves: The investigated storage and memory growth have distinct observed owners/mechanisms.
evidence.doesNotProve: That cache I/O had no indirect latency/page-cache effect or that all leaks are fixed.

evidence.signal: A bounded canary processes representative batches, reaches a stable memory plateau below the reviewed limit, emits zero new OOM kills/duplicates, drains the queue, and passes payment reconciliation for 60 minutes.
evidence.proves: The canary met declared guardrails for that cohort and window.
evidence.doesNotProve: Fleet-scale or long-duration safety, unseen payload distributions, or mastery.

followUps.prompt: What is the difference between memory request and limit in Kubernetes?
followUps.answer: A request primarily informs scheduling and, with other settings, quality-of-service treatment; a limit is an enforced maximum represented through cgroup configuration. Exact behavior depends on platform/version and memory management. A request is not a reservation of private physical RAM, and a limit does not reveal the correct working set.

followUps.prompt: Why can a container show more or less memory than one process RSS?
followUps.answer: The cgroup can contain several processes and charges categories beyond one process RSS, including file cache and some kernel memory depending on system/version. Shared pages, accounting definitions, and sampling time differ. Compare scoped cgroup counters with process breakdown; do not add unlike metrics blindly.

followUps.prompt: Would a health check prevent this OOM?
followUps.answer: No. A health check reports a probe result and may trigger orchestration decisions. It neither bounds memory nor proves business progress. An overloaded process can answer a shallow probe until killed, and an unhealthy label does not automatically recover state.

followUps.prompt: Should logs go to a Docker volume?
followUps.answer: Usually applications write bounded structured events to stdout/stderr and the platform logging pipeline owns rotation and retention. A volume may be required for specific audit or application contracts, but it needs capacity, ownership, backup, security, and lifecycle design; it is not a substitute for log management.

followUps.prompt: When is raising the memory limit correct?
followUps.answer: When representative measurement shows the legitimate bounded working set plus headroom exceeds the old limit, the node/fleet can support the new aggregate demand, application growth is controlled, and rollout guardrails exist. It may accompany a code fix; it is not a diagnosis by itself.

rubric.observableEvidence: Correlates 137, SIGKILL, OOMKilled and cgroup events without treating one field as universal proof.
Separates host/cgroup memory, process accounting, writable-layer storage, PID 1 behavior, and user-operation state.
Stops replay, preserves evidence, reconciles work, bounds canary/concurrency, and justifies resource changes.
Checks original payments, duplicates, queue, memory plateau, OOM events, layer growth, and interruption behavior.
Covers code/profile fixes, backpressure, durable state, PID1, filesystem/mounts, telemetry, limits, testing, and rollout.
